concepts.title: Lift
concepts.hook: A paper glider has no engine, yet its wing can hold it up while air moves past. When it slows, that upward force fades.
concepts.rule: A wing makes lift when air flows past it and is turned down. The air pushes the wing up. If nothing else changes, lift grows with speed squared, and in steady level flight it equals weight.

claims.text: Lift needs air moving past a wing. No air or no motion means no lift, and it does not matter whether the wing or the air is moving.
A wing turns the air that flows past it, and the air pushes back on the wing. That push is lift.
The idea that air over the top must meet the air below at the back edge is wrong. Thin wings with the same length on top and bottom still lift.
If nothing else changes, lift grows with the square of the speed, so twice the speed gives four times the lift.
In steady cruise, a plane's lift equals its weight, so a plane must reach the speed where its lift can equal its weight.

items.stem: Isha says a wing would lift even better on the Moon, since there is no air there to slow it down. What is not quite right?

options.text: No air drag, true, but no air means no lift either.
options.feedback: With no air to turn, a wing on the Moon makes no lift at any speed, so it cannot fly there.

options.text: The Moon pulls harder, so the wing would sink faster.
options.feedback: The Moon's pull is weaker than Earth's. The real problem is that it has no air to turn.

options.text: A wing lifts the same anywhere it moves fast enough.
options.feedback: Speed alone is not enough. A wing needs air flowing past it, and the Moon has none.

items.stem: At Delhi airport, Om sees planes take off facing into a strong wind. He thinks the wind must hold them back and make the run longer. What really happens?

options.text: The wind adds air past the wings, so they lift off sooner.
options.feedback: Lift needs air moving past the wing, whether the plane or the air moves, so a headwind helps it lift off.

options.text: The wind holds them back, so the run gets much longer.
options.feedback: The wind does push on the plane, but it also sends air over the wings, so less ground speed is needed.

options.text: The wind makes no difference, since engine speed is what counts.
options.feedback: What counts for lift is air moving past the wings, and the wind adds to that.

items.stem: In a hostel room, a table fan spins its tilted blades and pushes air out toward the bed. What does that air do to the blades?

options.text: It pushes back on them, the opposite way.
options.feedback: Push air one way and it pushes back the other way. Fan blades and wings both work like this.

options.text: No push, since air is far too light.
options.feedback: Air is light, but turning lots of it makes a real push back on the blades.

options.text: It pulls the blades along in the same direction.
options.feedback: The push on the blades points opposite to the air they throw, not with it.

items.stem: A thin, curved wing is the same length on top and bottom. Can it still lift?

options.text: Yes, tilted, it still turns the air down.
options.feedback: Any surface that turns air makes lift. Wing length on top and bottom does not matter.

options.text: No, the top must be longer than the bottom.
options.feedback: That comes from the equal-time story, which is wrong. Thin plates with equal lengths still lift.

options.text: Yes, if the air on top can race to catch up.
options.feedback: Air on top does not have to meet the air below. The wing lifts by turning air down.

items.stem: A loaded plane weighs twice as much, so it needs twice the lift to take off. About how many times faster must it go, all else the same?

options.text: About 1.4 times as fast.
options.feedback: Lift grows with speed squared, and 1.4 times 1.4 is about 2, so 1.4 times the speed doubles the lift.

options.text: About 2 times as fast.
options.feedback: Twice the speed gives four times the lift, which is more than needed. About 1.4 times is enough.

options.text: About 4 times as fast.
options.feedback: That would give sixteen times the lift. Since 1.4 times 1.4 is about 2, 1.4 times is enough.

items.stem: Why does a big plane need a long runway before it can leave the ground?

options.text: It must speed up until its wings make lift equal to its weight.
options.feedback: Lift needs air flowing past the wings, and it grows fast with speed. The runway gives room to reach that speed.

options.text: The engines need a long run to warm up before they push.
options.feedback: Engines push from the start. The run is about reaching the speed where lift equals weight.

options.text: The runway slope tips its nose up once it is long enough.
options.feedback: Runways are flat. The plane lifts off once its speed makes enough lift for its weight.

misconceptions.name: Shape alone lifts
misconceptions.correction: A still wing needs moving air to make lift.

misconceptions.name: Air is not pushed
misconceptions.correction: Wings turn air; the air pushes back on them.

misconceptions.name: Equal time on top
misconceptions.correction: Air on top does not have to meet the air below. Wings with equal top and bottom lengths lift too.

misconceptions.name: Lift keeps pace with speed
misconceptions.correction: Lift grows with speed times speed, so double speed gives four times the lift.

misconceptions.name: A headwind only slows a takeoff
misconceptions.correction: Wind blowing at the front of a plane adds air flowing past its wings, so it can lift off at a lower ground speed.

quest.title: Try a paper wing
quest.detail: Fold a paper glider. Watch what happens as it slows. Mark the air flow and the lift path on a sketch.

steps.title: Lift needs moving air

hook.stem: A kite lies flat on the grass on a still day. What does it need before it can rise?

options.text: Air moving past it.
options.feedback: Right. A kite or wing only lifts when air flows past it.

options.text: A lighter, thinner frame.
options.feedback: A light frame helps, but with no moving air even a light kite makes no lift.

options.text: A hot, sunny sky.
options.feedback: Sunshine does not lift a kite. It needs air flowing past it.

steps.teach: A wing lifts only when air flows past it, because lift is the air pushing on the wing. Move the wing, or let wind blow over it. No moving air means no lift.

example.ask: Tap what makes the lift.
parts: Riya runs across the school ground,
so air rushes over her paper glider's wings,
and it floats up out of her hand.
example.spot: so air rushes over her paper glider's wings,
example.feedback: Air moving over the wings makes the lift. Without that flow, the glider just drops.

guided.stem: A plane sits parked in calm air with its engines off. How much lift do its wings make?
guided.hint: Is anything moving past the wings?

options.text: None, or almost none.
options.feedback: Yes. With no air moving past, the wings make no real lift.

options.text: Full lift, just like in flight.
options.feedback: Lift needs moving air. A parked plane in calm air has almost none.

options.text: About half of its weight.
options.feedback: Nothing is flowing past the wings, so they make almost no lift.

steps.takeaway: No moving air, no lift.

steps.title: A wing turns air down, and the air pushes it up

hook.stem: You hold a flat card in front of a table fan, tipped up a little. Where does the air go after it hits the card?

options.text: Down, and the card gets pushed up.
options.feedback: Right. The card turns the air down, so the air pushes the card up.

options.text: Up, and it drags the card up with it.
options.feedback: The tipped card sends air down, not up. The push back on the card is upward.

options.text: Nowhere, it just slows down and stops.
options.feedback: The air is turned, not just slowed. Turning it down pushes the card up.

steps.teach: A tilted wing bends the passing air downward. Push air one way and it pushes back the other way, so the wing is pushed up. That push is lift. The 'air on top must catch up' story is wrong.

example.ask: Tap the push that lifts the kite.
parts: A kite tilts into the wind,
it bends the air downward,
and the air shoves the kite upward.
example.spot: and the air shoves the kite upward.
example.feedback: The kite turns air down, so the air pushes the kite up. That upward push is lift.

guided.stem: A wing is set to turn air upward instead of down. Which way does the force on the wing point?
guided.hint: The force points the other way from the turned air.

options.text: Downward.
options.feedback: Right. Turn air up and the air pushes the wing down.

options.text: Upward.
options.feedback: The push on the wing is opposite to the turned air, so it points down.

options.text: No force on the wing.
options.feedback: Turning air makes a push back, and here it points down.

steps.takeaway: A wing turns air down; the air pushes the wing up.

steps.title: More speed gives much more lift

hook.stem: A glider doubles its speed with its wings tilted the same. Guess how its lift changes.

options.text: About four times as much.
options.feedback: Right. Lift grows with speed times speed, so double speed gives four times.

options.text: About twice as much, in step with speed.
options.feedback: Lift grows faster than speed. Double speed gives about four times the lift.

options.text: It stays about the same.
options.feedback: Faster air past the wing means more lift, about four times here.

steps.teach: Faster air hits the wing more often and harder, so lift grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed gives four times the lift, at the same tilt. A plane must go fast before lift can carry its weight.

example.ask: Tap the cause of the bigger lift.
parts: A jet rolls slowly down the runway,
then it reaches twice that speed,
and its wings now make four times the lift.
example.spot: then it reaches twice that speed,
example.feedback: Doubling the speed is the cause. Lift grows with speed squared, so it becomes four times bigger.

guided.stem: A plane flies at three times its slowest speed. How much more lift can its wings make, all else equal?
guided.hint: Multiply the speed change by itself.

options.text: Nine times.
options.feedback: Right. Three times three is nine, so lift grows ninefold.

options.text: Three times.
options.feedback: Lift grows with speed squared, so triple speed gives nine times.

options.text: Six times.
options.feedback: Square the speed change: three times three is nine, not six.

steps.takeaway: Double the speed, four times the lift.

concepts.title: How a multirotor turns
concepts.hook: A quadcopter can spin in place while its four rotors stay flat. It does this by changing how hard each pair of rotors twists.
concepts.rule: A multirotor changes motor speeds to shift its push. A push gap between sides tilts it in pitch or roll, and the tilt moves it. Speeding one spinning pair and slowing the other turns its nose (yaw).

claims.text: To tilt in pitch or roll, the rotors on one side of a drone push harder than the rotors on the other side.
To turn its nose (yaw), a drone speeds up one spinning pair and slows the other, which keeps the total push steady.
Two rotors spin clockwise and two spin anticlockwise, so their twists on the body cancel.
To hover, the total upward push of the rotors equals the weight, and each rotor gives the same push, so each carries about a quarter.
Every pitch or roll also aims part of the push sideways, so a tilted drone starts to move.

items.stem: At a college drone club, one rotor of a four-rotor drone stops in a hover. Each rotor can give at most 30% of the weight. Predict what happens.

options.text: It sinks, since three rotors give at most 90%.
options.feedback: Three rotors at 30% each give 90% of the weight, less than the full weight, so it cannot hold its height.

options.text: It holds on, since three rotors can share it.
options.feedback: Sharing works only if they can push enough. At 30% each, three give 90%, short of the weight.

options.text: It climbs, since less weight sits on the rotors.
options.feedback: The drone weighs the same. With only 90% of its weight in push, it sinks.

items.stem: A small bag is hung under a hovering drone. Riya says hovering costs no extra push, so the rotors can stay as they are. What is not quite right?

options.text: All four must push harder to match the new weight.
options.feedback: In a hover the total push equals the weight. A heavier drone needs more push from every rotor.

options.text: Just the front rotors need to push harder.
options.feedback: That would tip the nose up. All four speed up together to stay level.

options.text: The rotors should slow down to save the battery.
options.feedback: Slowing down would make it sink. A heavier drone needs more push, not less.

items.stem: In a college lab, a breeze keeps pushing a hovering drone to the right. To hold its place it must push back to the left. How must it tilt?

options.text: Lean left, with its right rotors pushing harder.
options.feedback: The right side rises, the drone leans left, and part of its push now points left against the breeze.

options.text: Lean right, with its left rotors pushing harder.
options.feedback: Leaning right aims its push to the right, the same way as the breeze.

options.text: Stay level and just turn its nose left.
options.feedback: Turning the nose does not push it sideways. It has to tilt left.

items.stem: Why does a drone that tips its nose down also start to fly forward?

options.text: Its push now points partly forward.
options.feedback: Tilting aims part of the rotor push ahead, so the drone speeds forward.

options.text: Its front rotors pull it along like a car.
options.feedback: Rotors push along their own axis, which is mostly up. The tilt aims some push forward.

options.text: Gravity drags the lower nose ahead.
options.feedback: Gravity pulls straight down. Forward motion comes from the tilted push.

items.stem: A 20 newton drone hovers. To turn, its clockwise rotors speed up to 6 newtons each. About how hard must each anticlockwise rotor push to keep its height?

options.text: About 4 newtons.
options.feedback: The total must stay 20 newtons. The fast pair gives 12, so the slow pair shares 8, about 4 each.

options.text: About 5 newtons.
options.feedback: That is the hover share. With the fast pair at 12, the slow pair must drop to 8 in all.

options.text: About 6 newtons.
options.feedback: Then all four push equally, so the twists cancel and it does not turn. The slow pair gives about 4.

items.stem: In the hostel, a table fan stands on a smooth, slippery tray. Predict which way its base tends to twist as the blades spin up.

options.text: The opposite way to the blades.
options.feedback: A spinning blade twists the body that drives it the opposite way, just like a drone rotor does.

options.text: The same way as the blades.
options.feedback: The air pushes back on the blades, so the body that turns them is twisted the opposite way.

options.text: It does not twist, since fans are heavy.
options.feedback: A heavy base resists, but the twist is still there, and on a slippery tray it shows.

misconceptions.name: Hovering takes no push
misconceptions.correction: A hovering drone pushes up as hard as it weighs, so extra weight needs extra push.

misconceptions.name: All speeds same for a turn
misconceptions.correction: A turn needs a change in the balance of motor speeds.

misconceptions.name: Drones bank to turn their nose
misconceptions.correction: A drone turns its nose on the spot by changing the twist balance. Tilting is what moves it sideways.

misconceptions.name: Tilt is only for balance
misconceptions.correction: Tilting points part of the push sideways, which is how a drone moves.

steps.title: Four rotors share the weight

hook.stem: A drone that weighs 2 newtons hovers on four equal rotors. How hard does each rotor push up?

options.text: About 0.5 newtons.
options.feedback: Right. Four rotors share 2 newtons, so each gives about half a newton.

options.text: About 2 newtons each.
options.feedback: That is the whole weight. Split four ways, each rotor gives 0.5 newtons.

options.text: About 8 newtons.
options.feedback: That is four times too much. The rotors share the weight, about 0.5 each.

steps.teach: To hover, the four rotors together push up (thrust) as hard as the drone weighs, so each one carries about a quarter. Speed them all up equally and it climbs straight up.

example.ask: Tap what makes the drone climb.
parts: The drone hovers over the cricket pitch,
then all four rotors speed up together,
and it rises straight up.
example.spot: then all four rotors speed up together,
example.feedback: Speeding all four rotors equally lifts the total push above the weight, so it climbs without tilting.

guided.stem: All four rotors slow down by the same amount. What does a hovering drone do?
guided.hint: Compare the total push with the weight.

options.text: It sinks, still level.
options.feedback: Right. Less total push than weight means it moves down, and equal slowing keeps it level.

options.text: It tips its nose forward.
options.feedback: Tipping needs uneven push. Equal slowing just makes it sink.

options.text: It spins slowly in place.
options.feedback: Spinning needs the two spinning pairs unbalanced. Equal slowing makes it sink.

steps.takeaway: In a hover, four rotors share the weight equally.

steps.title: Uneven push tilts the drone, and the tilt moves it

hook.stem: The two back rotors of a drone push harder than the front two. What does it do first?

options.text: Tips its nose down.
options.feedback: Right. The back rises, so the nose dips.

options.text: Tips its nose up.
options.feedback: The harder-pushing back end rises, so the nose goes down, not up.

options.text: Spins on the spot.
options.feedback: Spinning comes from the spinning pairs. A front and back gap tilts it.

steps.teach: Push harder on one side and that side rises, so the drone tilts. A tilted drone aims part of its push sideways, so it starts to move that way.

example.ask: Tap the cause of the tilt.
parts: At a college drone race, a quad leans left
because its right rotors push harder,
and then it slides to the left.
example.spot: because its right rotors push harder,
example.feedback: Extra push on the right lifts that side, so the drone rolls left and slides that way.

guided.stem: A drone needs to roll to its right. Which rotors should push harder?
guided.hint: Which side has to rise?

options.text: The left rotors.
options.feedback: Right. The left side rises, so the drone tips to the right.

options.text: The right rotors.
options.feedback: That lifts the right side, which tips the drone to the left.

options.text: Each of the four, equally.
options.feedback: Equal push keeps it level. A roll needs one side to push harder.

steps.takeaway: Uneven push tilts it; the tilt sends it sideways.

steps.title: Opposite spins let it turn on the spot

hook.stem: Why do two of a drone's rotors spin clockwise and two anticlockwise?

options.text: So their twists on the body cancel.
options.feedback: Right. Each rotor twists the body; the two pairs cancel out.

options.text: So the drone can fly faster.
options.feedback: It is not about speed. Opposite spins stop the body from twisting.

options.text: So the blades do not hit each other.
options.feedback: Spacing keeps blades apart. Opposite spins cancel the twist on the body.

steps.teach: Each spinning rotor twists the drone's body the opposite way. Two spin each way, so the twists cancel. Speed up one pair and slow the other, and the drone turns on the spot.

example.ask: Tap why the drone turns.
parts: A hovering drone keeps its height,
but its clockwise pair speeds up while the other pair slows,
so its nose swings around.
example.spot: but its clockwise pair speeds up while the other pair slows,
example.feedback: The faster pair twists the body more than the slower pair, so the drone turns its nose.

guided.stem: All four rotors on a test drone spin the same way. What happens to its body?
guided.hint: Is anything left to cancel the twist?

options.text: It keeps turning the opposite way.
options.feedback: Right. With no opposite pair, the twist is never cancelled, so the body spins.

options.text: It stays still, since four twists balance.
options.feedback: Four twists in the same direction add up, so the body turns.

options.text: It flips over onto its back.
options.feedback: The twist is about the up-down line, so the body spins, not flips.

steps.takeaway: Two pairs spin opposite ways; speed one, slow one, to turn.

concepts.title: Batteries and flight time
concepts.hook: Doubling a drone battery does not double flight time. The bigger battery is heavier, so the motors work harder.
concepts.rule: Flight time is battery energy divided by the power used. More battery adds energy and weight, and hover power rises faster than weight, so in the simple model flight time peaks and then falls.

claims.text: Flight time depends on stored energy and the rate at which it is used.
A heavy battery adds weight, so the craft needs more lift.
In the hover model, power grows as thrust to the power 1.5, so it climbs faster than weight.
In the simple model, flight time rises with battery size only up to a peak, when the battery is about two thirds of the drone's mass. Past that, more battery cuts time.
In a Berkeley test, small drones flew fresh batteries to a main drone, which then hovered 57 minutes instead of 12.

items.stem: Kunal's phone battery stores about 15 watt-hours, and a game drains it at about 5 watts. Using the same energy-over-power rule as a drone battery, about how many hours can he play?

options.text: About 3 hours.
options.feedback: Energy over power works for any battery: 15 watt-hours at 5 watts lasts about 3 hours.

options.text: About 75 hours.
options.feedback: That multiplies the numbers. Divide energy by power: 15 by 5 is 3 hours.

options.text: About 20 hours.
options.feedback: That adds the numbers. Divide energy by power: 15 by 5 is about 3 hours.

items.stem: For a college project, Rahul picks the drone with the higher hover power, since more power must mean a longer flight. What is not quite right?

options.text: More power empties the same battery sooner.
options.feedback: Power is how fast energy is spent. With the same battery, the higher-power drone lands first.

options.text: Power has no real link to flight time.
options.feedback: Power matters a lot: flight time is energy divided by power.

options.text: Higher power means a longer flight, but slower.
options.feedback: Higher power spends energy faster, so the flight is shorter, not longer.

items.stem: A college team adds a camera that doubles its drone weight but keeps the same battery. Predict the new hover time, in the simple model.

options.text: Roughly a third of before.
options.feedback: Twice the weight needs nearly three times the power, and the same energy at triple power lasts about a third as long.

options.text: About half of before, in step with weight.
options.feedback: Power rises faster than weight, nearly threefold, so time drops to about a third.

options.text: The same as before.
options.feedback: The battery is the same, but the heavier drone spends its energy much faster.

items.stem: Sana swaps her drone battery for one that stores twice the energy but weighs twice as much. Does it fly twice as long?

options.text: No, less than twice, since the extra weight raises the power.
options.feedback: Double energy would double time only at the same power. The heavier battery makes the motors use more power.

options.text: Yes, twice the energy gives twice the flight time.
options.feedback: That holds only if power stays the same. The extra weight pushes the power up.

options.text: No, any bigger battery gives a shorter flight than the old one.
options.feedback: A bigger battery can still help, up to a point. It just gives less than double.

items.stem: Why does flight time fall once the battery is more than about two thirds of a drone's mass?

options.text: The extra weight costs more power than its energy adds.
options.feedback: Past the peak, each added gram of battery raises hover power more than it adds energy.

options.text: Big batteries hold less energy in each kilogram they weigh.
options.feedback: The model keeps energy per kilogram fixed. The weight cost is what wins.

options.text: The motors get weaker as they get older.
options.feedback: Motor age is not the cause. Extra weight costs more power than it adds.

items.stem: A college team's drone carries a battery that is 80% of its mass. They want the longest hover from the same drone. What should they try?

options.text: A smaller battery, closer to two thirds of the mass.
options.feedback: At 80% it is past the peak, so a lighter battery saves more power than the energy it gives up.

options.text: A bigger battery, to store as much energy as they can.
options.feedback: Past the peak, more battery cuts time. Moving back toward two thirds helps.

options.text: The same battery, since the size makes no difference.
options.feedback: Size matters a lot here. Past two thirds, the extra weight costs more than it gives.

misconceptions.name: Double size, double time
misconceptions.correction: More battery adds weight, so time need not scale with size.

misconceptions.name: Weight costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: More weight needs more lift and motor work.

misconceptions.name: Power keeps pace with weight
misconceptions.correction: Hover power rises faster than weight, so twice the weight needs nearly three times the power.

misconceptions.name: More power means longer flight
misconceptions.correction: Power is how fast energy is spent, so more power empties the same battery sooner.

steps.title: Flight time is energy divided by power

hook.stem: A drone battery stores 50 watt-hours and the drone hovers at 100 watts. How long can it hover?

options.text: About half an hour.
options.feedback: Right. 50 divided by 100 is half an hour.

options.text: About 2 hours, maybe more.
options.feedback: That flips the sum. 50 watt-hours at 100 watts lasts half an hour.

options.text: About 50 minutes.
options.feedback: Divide energy by power: 50 by 100 gives half an hour, about 30 minutes.

steps.teach: A battery is a store of energy, and the motors spend it at a rate called power. So flight time is energy divided by power: spend it faster and the time shrinks.

example.ask: Tap the rate of use.
parts: Meera's drone battery holds 60 watt-hours,
its motors draw 120 watts in a hover,
so it can hover for about half an hour.
example.spot: its motors draw 120 watts in a hover,
example.feedback: Watts tell how fast energy is used. 60 watt-hours at 120 watts lasts half an hour.

guided.stem: A team wants its drone to fly twice as long. Which plan works?
guided.hint: Look at the two numbers in the division.

options.text: Double the energy, or halve the power.
options.feedback: Right. Time is energy over power, so either change doubles it, if nothing else shifts.

options.text: Double both the energy and the power used.
options.feedback: Doubling both leaves energy over power the same, so the time does not change.

options.text: Halve the energy and double the power.
options.feedback: That cuts the time to a quarter. Energy goes up or power goes down to fly longer.

steps.takeaway: Flight time is stored energy divided by power used.

steps.title: Extra weight costs even more power

hook.stem: A drone gets twice as heavy. Guess the power it needs to hover.

options.text: More than twice as much.
options.feedback: Right. Hover power climbs faster than weight, nearly three times here.

options.text: Twice as much, in step with weight.
options.feedback: Power grows faster than weight. Twice the weight needs nearly three times.

options.text: The same as before.
options.feedback: More weight needs more push, and power climbs even faster than push.

steps.teach: A heavier drone needs more push to hover, and in the hover model power rises faster than push. So twice the weight needs nearly three times the power, and the flight gets much shorter.

example.ask: Tap the hidden extra cost.
parts: A delivery drone picks up a heavy parcel,
its rotors push harder to hold it up,
and its hover power rises even faster than its weight.
example.spot: and its hover power rises even faster than its weight.
example.feedback: The weight goes up, but hover power goes up faster still, so flight time drops sharply.

guided.stem: A drone's weight doubles, then doubles again. About how much more hover power does it need in all?
guided.hint: Apply the nearly-3x jump once for each doubling.

options.text: About 8 times.
options.feedback: Right. Nearly 3 times, then nearly 3 times again, comes to about 8.

options.text: About 4 times.
options.feedback: Power climbs faster than weight. Four times the weight needs about 8 times the power.

options.text: About 6 times.
options.feedback: The jumps multiply, they do not add. Nearly 3 times nearly 3 is about 8.

steps.takeaway: More weight needs more push, and power rises even faster.

steps.title: Bigger batteries hit a limit

hook.stem: Keep adding battery to a drone. What happens to its flight time?

options.text: It rises, then peaks, then falls.
options.feedback: Right. At first extra energy wins; later the extra weight costs more.

options.text: It keeps rising, a little less each time.
options.feedback: Extra battery adds weight, and past a point the weight wins, so time falls.

options.text: It stays the same.
options.feedback: Small batteries gain a lot from more energy. Time rises before it peaks.

steps.teach: Each extra bit of battery adds energy but also weight, and weight costs power. So in the simple model, flight time peaks when the battery is about two thirds of the mass, then falls.

example.ask: Tap the limit they had to get around.
parts: Berkeley engineers wanted a drone to hover much longer.
A bigger battery would push it past the peak.
So small drones flew fresh batteries to it.
example.spot: A bigger battery would push it past the peak.
example.feedback: Past about two thirds battery, more battery cuts time. Swapping batteries in flight gave 57 minutes of hover instead of 12.

guided.stem: A drone weighs 3 kg in all, and 1 kg of that is battery. Is it past the peak?
guided.hint: Work out what share of the mass is battery.

options.text: No, it is still below the peak.
options.feedback: Right. One third is well below two thirds, so more battery still helps.

options.text: Yes, it is well past the peak.
options.feedback: One third is below two thirds, so it has not reached the peak yet.

options.text: It sits right on the peak already.
options.feedback: The peak is near two thirds battery. This drone is at one third.

steps.takeaway: Past about two thirds battery, more battery means less flight.

concepts.title: Flight sensors
concepts.hook: A roof can block a drone's GPS signal. Yet the drone still feels a quick tilt.
concepts.rule: A gyroscope senses turning, and an accelerometer senses speed changes and helps give tilt. GPS times satellite signals to find position. A barometer reads air pressure, which falls with height. Each clue has limits.

claims.text: A gyroscope senses how fast the drone turns. An accelerometer senses changes in speed and is used to work out tilt.
GPS works out position from how long satellite radio signals take to arrive.
GPS phones are usually within 4.9 metres under open sky, but buildings, trees and indoor use make it worse.
Air pressure falls as you go higher, because there is less air above, so a barometer can track height. Weather also changes air pressure a little.
The standard air pressure at sea level is about 1013 hPa.

items.stem: Ravi says a drone needs GPS to know it is tilting. What is not quite right?

options.text: Its gyroscope and accelerometer sense tilting, with no signal needed.
options.feedback: Turning and tilt are sensed on board. GPS only helps with position, and it needs a clear sky.

options.text: GPS senses tilt, but just when the sky is clear.
options.feedback: GPS gives position, not tilt. The on-board motion sensors sense tilting.

options.text: Drones do not tilt in flight, so they need no sensor.
options.feedback: Drones tilt all the time to move. The gyroscope and accelerometer sense it.

items.stem: In a college lab, Neha reads a drone's flight log. The gyroscope shows a fast turn, but GPS shows no change in place. What was the drone doing?

options.text: Turning on the spot.
options.feedback: The gyroscope senses turning while GPS shows the place stayed the same, so it spun where it was.

options.text: Flying fast in a straight line.
options.feedback: Then GPS would show its place changing, and the gyroscope would show little turning.

options.text: Climbing straight up quickly.
options.feedback: A climb is a change in height, not a turn. The gyroscope reading says it was turning.

items.stem: On a covered train platform, the dot showing Priya in her cab app keeps jumping around. Why?

options.text: The roof blocks and bounces the satellite signals.
options.feedback: Phones use GPS too. Roofs and walls block or bounce the signals, so the position wanders.

options.text: The trains confuse her phone's motion sensors.
options.feedback: Motion sensors sense turning, not place. The roof is upsetting the GPS signals.

options.text: The cab app checks her place once a minute.
options.feedback: Timing of the app is not the issue here. The roof is blocking the satellite signals.

items.stem: A drone uses phone-grade GPS alone to land in the middle of a pad, under open sky. About how many metres off its mark could it typically land?

options.text: About 5 metres.
options.feedback: Phone-grade GPS is typically within about 4.9 metres under open sky, so a GPS-only landing can miss by that much.

options.text: About 1 centimetre.
options.feedback: GPS is not that exact. Under open sky a phone is usually within about 5 metres.

options.text: About 500 metres.
options.feedback: That is far too loose. Under open sky a phone is usually within about 5 metres.

items.stem: Why does air pressure drop as a drone climbs?

options.text: There is less air above it pressing down.
options.feedback: Higher up there are fewer air molecules, so the air presses less and the pressure falls.

options.text: The Sun heats the air more up there.
options.feedback: Heat is not the reason. There is less air higher up, so pressure falls.

options.text: The spinning rotors push the nearby air away.
options.feedback: Rotors move air nearby, but pressure falls with height for every object, drone or not.

items.stem: Which line best explains how one drone knows its tilt, place and height?

options.text: Motion sensors give tilt, GPS gives place, and the barometer gives height.
options.feedback: Each sensor gives one clue, and the drone's computer combines them, since none can do all three.

options.text: GPS alone gives its tilt, its place and its height.
options.feedback: GPS gives position. Motion sensors give tilt, and the barometer tracks height.

options.text: The barometer covers tilt, place and height from air pressure.
options.feedback: A barometer reads air pressure, which tracks height. Other sensors do the rest.

misconceptions.name: GPS senses all turns
misconceptions.correction: The gyroscope senses quick turns; GPS gives position.

misconceptions.name: One sensor is perfect
misconceptions.correction: GPS can drift near buildings and indoors, so drones mix several sensors.

misconceptions.name: Pressure is the same at every height
misconceptions.correction: Air pressure drops as you climb, which lets a barometer track height.

quest.title: Make a sensor map
quest.detail: On paper, draw a drone and link tilt, place and height to the motion sensors, GPS and barometer. Add one limit for each.

Gyroscope-for-tilt wording fixed: the gyroscope senses turn rate and the accelerometer is used for tilt.

steps.title: Motion sensors feel every tilt

hook.stem: A drone hovers in a school hall with no GPS signal. A gust tilts it. Which sensor notices the turn?

options.text: The gyroscope on board.
options.feedback: Right. The gyroscope senses how fast the drone turns, signal or not.

options.text: The GPS, from the satellites.
options.feedback: GPS gives position, and here it has no signal. The gyroscope feels the turn.

options.text: The barometer.
options.feedback: A barometer reads air pressure for height. The gyroscope senses turning.

steps.teach: The drone's small computer has a gyroscope, which senses how fast it turns, and an accelerometer, which senses speed changes and helps give its tilt. Both sit on board, so they work indoors with no signal.

example.ask: Tap the part that senses the turn.
parts: A gust hits the drone in the hall,
its gyroscope reads a fast roll,
and the motors level it out.
example.spot: its gyroscope reads a fast roll,
example.feedback: The gyroscope measures how fast the drone turns, so the motors can correct the roll.

guided.stem: A drone speeds up from rest. Which sensor feels the change in its motion?
guided.hint: Which one measures changes in speed?

options.text: The accelerometer.
options.feedback: Right. The accelerometer measures changing speed, so it feels the speed-up.

options.text: The barometer, from the air.
options.feedback: A barometer reads air pressure for height. The accelerometer feels the speed-up.

options.text: The GPS.
options.feedback: GPS gives position from satellites. The accelerometer senses the change in motion.

steps.takeaway: Motion sensors on board feel each tilt, with no signal needed.

steps.title: GPS times signals from space

hook.stem: How does a GPS receiver find where it is?

options.text: It times radio signals from satellites.
options.feedback: Right. It turns each signal's travel time into a distance.

options.text: It sends a photo up to a satellite.
options.feedback: GPS sends no photos. The receiver times signals from satellites.

options.text: It reads the Earth's magnetism, like a compass.
options.feedback: That is what a compass does. GPS times satellite radio signals.

steps.teach: GPS satellites send radio signals all the time. A receiver times how long each takes to arrive, which gives its distance to each satellite, so it finds where it is, to about 5 metres in open sky.

example.ask: Tap the timing step.
parts: Signals from several satellites reach the drone,
it measures how long each one took,
and turns those times into its position.
example.spot: it measures how long each one took,
example.feedback: Timing each signal gives the distance to each satellite, and those distances fix the position.

guided.stem: A drone flies between tall buildings. What happens to its GPS fix?
guided.hint: What can walls do to a radio signal?

options.text: It gets less accurate.
options.feedback: Right. Blocked and bouncing signals make the position worse.

options.text: It gets more accurate.
options.feedback: Buildings block and bounce signals, so the fix gets worse.

options.text: It stays just as good.
options.feedback: Buildings block and bounce the signals, so the fix gets worse.

steps.takeaway: GPS turns signal travel times into a position.

steps.title: Air pressure tells the height

hook.stem: You carry a barometer up a tall building. What happens to the air pressure it reads?

options.text: It goes down.
options.feedback: Right. Air pressure falls as you go higher.

options.text: It goes up.
options.feedback: Higher up there is less air, so the pressure reading drops.

options.text: It stays the same.
options.feedback: Pressure changes with height. It falls as you climb.

steps.teach: Air pressure is the push of the air above you. Climb higher and there is less air above, so pressure drops. A barometer reads it to track height, but weather also shifts pressure a little, so the reading can drift.

example.ask: Tap the clue the barometer uses.
parts: A drone climbs above the school roof,
its barometer reads a small drop in air pressure,
so it knows it has gone higher.
example.spot: its barometer reads a small drop in air pressure,
example.feedback: A drop in air pressure means the drone is higher, so the barometer can track height.

guided.stem: A drone's barometer reads the same pressure as one on the ground beside it. Where is the drone?
guided.hint: Equal readings mean equal what?

options.text: About at ground level.
options.feedback: Right. Pressure changes with height, so the same reading means about the same height.

options.text: High above the ground.
options.feedback: Higher up, the pressure would read lower. The same reading means about the same height.

options.text: Far below the ground.
options.feedback: Lower down, the pressure would read higher. The same reading means the same height.

steps.takeaway: Pressure falls as you climb, so a barometer tracks height.

concepts.title: Why birds flap but planes do not
concepts.hook: A bird can flap for both lift and forward push; a jet keeps fixed wings while its engine supplies the forward push.
concepts.rule: A plane's fixed wings make most of its lift, while its engines beat drag. A bird has no engine, so its flapping wings make both lift and forward push, and the downstroke does most of the work.

claims.text: Bird wing flaps can provide lift and forward push.
A plane's wings make most of its lift, and its engines make thrust.
A plane's engine only has to beat drag, not lift the plane. Gliders fly with no engine at all.
At takeoff, small parrots tilt their wing strokes so lift points forward to speed up, and drag points up to hold nearly half their weight.
In small parrots, the downstroke uses nearly all the flapping power, while the upstroke costs almost none.
In steady cruise, thrust equals drag and lift equals weight.
When landing, small parrots aim their lift backward, which gives about a quarter of the braking force.

items.stem: A plane cruises at a steady speed and height. Its engines give 20,000 newtons of thrust. About how much drag must act on the plane?

options.text: About 20,000 newtons.
options.feedback: At a steady speed, thrust equals drag, so the drag is about 20,000 newtons.

options.text: About 40,000 newtons.
options.feedback: More drag than thrust would slow it down. In steady cruise the two are equal.

options.text: About 10,000 newtons.
options.feedback: If thrust beat drag by that much, the plane would keep speeding up. In steady cruise they match.

items.stem: In the school classroom, Arjun throws a paper plane. Predict what keeps it in the air once it leaves his hand.

options.text: Its wings lift as air flows past, with no engine.
options.feedback: A paper plane is a glider. Air flowing past its wings lifts it while it slowly glides down.

options.text: The push from Arjun's hand keeps lifting it up.
options.feedback: His throw gives it speed, but once it leaves his hand the wings make the lift.

options.text: The warm classroom air carries it like a balloon.
options.feedback: Paper is far denser than air. Air flowing past its wings is what lifts it.

items.stem: On a hostel balcony, a small pet parrot swoops in to land on a rail. Which way does it aim the lift from its wings?

options.text: Backward, to help it brake before the rail.
options.feedback: Lift does not always point up. When landing, small parrots aim it backward for about a quarter of the braking.

options.text: Straight up, as lift points up in flight.
options.feedback: Lift can be aimed. When landing, small parrots tilt it backward to help them slow down.

options.text: Forward, to keep its speed until it lands.
options.feedback: Forward lift speeds a bird up, which suits takeoff. To land, it aims lift backward.

items.stem: Sam says birds flap their wings just to stay up, the way you pump air into a tyre. What is not quite right?

options.text: Each tilted flap also pushes the bird forward.
options.feedback: A bird has no engine, so its flaps must give forward push as well as lift.

options.text: Birds flap to stay up, but glide to move ahead.
options.feedback: Gliding only uses speed it already has. The forward push comes from tilted flaps.

options.text: Birds flap to steer, not to stay up.
options.feedback: Flaps do lift the bird. They also push it forward, since it has no engine.

items.stem: Why does the downstroke use nearly all the power of a wingbeat?

options.text: It pushes hard on the air, while the upstroke is a light reset.
options.feedback: The downstroke does the hard pushing, so it uses nearly all the power. The upstroke costs almost none.

options.text: Gravity pulls the wing down, so it needs the most power.
options.feedback: Gravity helps a wing move down, if anything. The power goes into pushing on the air.

options.text: The upstroke is when the bird rests its whole body.
options.feedback: The upstroke is light, but the bird is still flying. The downstroke does the pushing.

items.stem: Match each flying part with its main job.

options.text: A plane's fixed wing
options.feedback: The fixed wing makes most of the lift as air flows past it.

options.text: Most of the lift
options.feedback: On a plane, most of the lift comes from the fixed wings.

options.text: A jet engine
options.feedback: An engine only has to push the plane forward against drag.

options.text: Beating air drag
options.feedback: That is the engine's whole job; the wings hold the plane up.

options.text: A small parrot's downstroke
options.feedback: The downstroke is the hard-working half of each wingbeat.

options.text: Nearly all the flap power
options.feedback: Almost all the work of each wingbeat is done on the way down.

misconceptions.name: All wings must flap
misconceptions.correction: A fixed wing can lift when air moves past it.

misconceptions.name: Engine makes all lift
misconceptions.correction: The engine gives forward thrust; the wing makes most lift.

misconceptions.name: Lift only points up
misconceptions.correction: Small parrots tilt their strokes so lift can point forward to speed up or backward to brake.

misconceptions.name: Thrust must beat drag in cruise
misconceptions.correction: At a steady speed, thrust equals drag. More thrust than drag would make the plane speed up.

misconceptions.name: Birds flap only to stay up
misconceptions.correction: A bird's tilted flaps also push it forward, since it has no engine.

sources.title: Birds repurpose the role of drag and lift to take off and land

quest.title: Spot two pushes
quest.detail: Watch a bird and a plane clip. Draw an arrow for forward push and one for lift on each.

steps.title: A plane splits the jobs: wings lift, engines beat drag

hook.stem: A jet's wings never flap. What keeps it up?

options.text: Air flowing past its wings.
options.feedback: Right. Moving air over the fixed wings makes most of the lift.

options.text: Its engines pushing it upward.
options.feedback: The engines push it forward. The wings make most of the lift.

options.text: Hot air trapped inside the cabin.
options.feedback: A plane is no hot-air balloon. Its wings make the lift.

steps.teach: Wings hold a plane up as air flows past them. Engines only push it forward against air drag, and at a steady speed the push equals the drag. So a glider, with no engine, still flies.

example.ask: Tap the part that holds the plane up.
parts: The jet's engines roar,
pushing it fast down the runway,
until air over its wings lifts it off.
example.spot: until air over its wings lifts it off.
example.feedback: The engines give speed, but the air flowing over the wings makes the lift.

guided.stem: A plane's engine stops high in the sky. What can its wings still do?
guided.hint: Think about whether air still moves past.

options.text: Keep making lift as it glides down.
options.feedback: Right. While air flows past, the wings keep lifting, so it glides.

options.text: No lift, so it drops like a stone.
options.feedback: The wings still lift as long as air flows past them.

options.text: Lift it higher for a while.
options.feedback: Without thrust it cannot climb, but the wings still let it glide.

steps.takeaway: Wings carry the weight; engines beat drag.

steps.title: A bird has no engine, so its wings push too

hook.stem: A bird has no engine. What pushes it forward as it takes off?

options.text: Its own flapping wings.
options.feedback: Right. Tilted flaps push air down and back, so the bird is lifted and pushed forward.

options.text: Wind under its tail feathers.
options.feedback: Birds take off in still air too. Their flapping wings give the push.

options.text: Its light, hollow bones.
options.feedback: Light bones help, but they push nothing. The flapping wings do.

steps.teach: A bird has no engine, so its wings must do both jobs. By tilting each stroke it aims the push: forward and up to take off, backward to brake when it lands.

example.ask: Tap the move that speeds it up.
parts: A small parrot leaps off its perch,
it tilts its wing strokes forward,
and it speeds up as it climbs.
example.spot: it tilts its wing strokes forward,
example.feedback: Tilting the strokes aims lift forward, so the bird speeds up as well as rising.

guided.stem: Why can't a bird just hold its wings still, like a plane, to take off?
guided.hint: Where would its forward push come from?

options.text: Nothing else would drive it ahead.
options.feedback: Right. A plane has engines for that. A bird must flap to make its own push.

options.text: Its wings are too small to lift a bird.
options.feedback: Bird wings do lift. What a still wing cannot give a bird is forward push.

options.text: Feathers stop air flowing past still wings.
options.feedback: Air flows past still feathers fine. The missing piece is forward push.

steps.takeaway: With no engine, a bird flaps to lift and push.

steps.title: The downstroke does most of the work

hook.stem: A small parrot flaps down, then up. Which half of the flap needs most of the power?

options.text: The downstroke.
options.feedback: Right. The downstroke uses nearly all the power of each wingbeat.

options.text: The upstroke.
options.feedback: The upstroke costs almost no power. The downstroke does the work.

options.text: Both need the same.
options.feedback: They are very unequal. The downstroke uses nearly all the power.

steps.teach: Each wingbeat has two halves. The downstroke pushes hard on the air, so it uses nearly all the power. The upstroke is a light reset that costs almost nothing.

example.ask: Tap the stroke that does the hard work.
parts: A small parrot beats its wings to take off,
its strong downstroke uses most of the power,
while its upstroke costs almost nothing.
example.spot: its strong downstroke uses most of the power,
example.feedback: The downstroke does nearly all the work. The upstroke costs almost no power.

guided.stem: A small parrot tires on a long flight. Which half of its flap is wearing it out?
guided.hint: Which half pushes hard on the air?

options.text: The downstroke.
options.feedback: Yes. The downstroke uses nearly all the power, so it does the tiring work.

options.text: The upstroke.
options.feedback: The upstroke is a light reset that costs almost no power.

options.text: Gliding between flaps.
options.feedback: Gliding uses little power. The downstroke does the hard work.

steps.takeaway: The downstroke does nearly all the work of a flap.

concepts.title: How a ceiling fan moves air
concepts.hook: A fan can cool sweaty skin in a warm classroom, yet the air stays warm. Where did the cooling happen?
concepts.rule: Spinning fan blades push room air along. The breeze mainly helps sweat dry, so people feel cooler, but the air does not get colder. Fans cool people, not rooms, and they help less in humid air.

claims.text: A ceiling fan moves room air with rotating blades.
A fan does not make cold air. It only moves the air already in the room.
Moving air helps sweat dry off your skin, which mainly is how a fan makes you feel cooler.
Fans cool people, not rooms, so a fan in an empty room does no good.
In winter, a fan that can reverse runs the other way to move warm air down from the ceiling.
When the air is humid, sweat dries off the body more slowly, so the body cools less.

items.stem: In a hostel room at 32°C, Vikram switches on the fan to cool the room. Predict the room thermometer after ten minutes.

options.text: About 32°C, much the same.
options.feedback: A fan moves the air but makes no cold air, so the room stays about as warm. Vikram feels cooler, though.

options.text: Down to about 28°C.
options.feedback: That would need a cooler or AC. A fan only moves the warm air around.

options.text: Down a little, since he feels cooler.
options.feedback: He feels cooler because sweat dries, but the air itself stays about as warm.

items.stem: In winter, someone runs a reversible ceiling fan the other way. What is it doing then?

options.text: Moving warm air down from near the ceiling.
options.feedback: Warm air rises. In winter, a reversed fan gently pushes it back down where people sit.

options.text: Making the room colder, so people sleep well.
options.feedback: Fans make no cold air. In winter the reversed fan moves warm ceiling air down.

options.text: Resting its motor for the next summer.
options.feedback: Running the other way is not a rest. It moves warm ceiling air down.

items.stem: During exam week, Arjun studies in his room but leaves the fan running in the empty common room "to keep it cool". What does that fan do?

options.text: Uses power but cools nobody.
options.feedback: Fans cool people, not rooms. With no one there to feel the breeze, it only uses power.

options.text: Keeps the common room air cooler for later.
options.feedback: A fan adds no cold to the air, so the empty room is just as warm later.

options.text: Dries the room so it feels cooler later.
options.feedback: Drying helps sweaty skin. With no one there, nothing is cooled.

items.stem: After a cricket match, Dev sits under the fan beside a dry steel water bottle. Predict which one ends up cooler than the room air.

options.text: Dev, since drying sweat takes heat from his skin.
options.feedback: The breeze is room air, so it cannot chill the dry bottle. Only Dev has sweat to dry, so only his skin cools.

options.text: The bottle, since steel feels cold to the touch.
options.feedback: Steel feels cold, but the breeze is room air. With nothing to dry, the bottle stays at room heat.

options.text: Both, since the fan blows on each the same.
options.feedback: The same room air blows on both, but only wet skin is cooled by drying.

items.stem: A weather app shows how hot it 'feels'. Two days are both near 38°C. In humid air, sweat and a fan cool you less, so the humid day feels like 51°C and the dry day like 36°C. About how many degrees hotter does the humid day feel?

options.text: About 15 degrees hotter.
options.feedback: 51 minus 36 is about 15. The air is equally hot, but slow-drying sweat makes the humid day feel far worse.

options.text: About 0 degrees, since both are 38°C.
options.feedback: The air matches, but humid air slows drying sweat, so the humid day feels about 15 degrees hotter.

options.text: About 51 degrees hotter.
options.feedback: 51°C is how the humid day feels, not the gap. The gap from 36°C is about 15 degrees.

items.stem: In a Mumbai hostel in the monsoon, the fan barely cools Kabir. Which change would make the same fan cool him more?

options.text: Drier air, so his sweat can dry faster.
options.feedback: Sweat dries faster in drier air, so the same breeze would take more heat from his skin.

options.text: Closing the windows to trap the breeze.
options.feedback: Trapping damp air keeps it damp. Drier air is what lets sweat dry faster.

options.text: A warmer room, so the breeze feels stronger.
options.feedback: More heat makes things worse. Drier air lets his sweat dry and cool him.

misconceptions.name: Fan makes cold air
misconceptions.correction: A fan moves the air already in the room; it makes none colder.

misconceptions.name: A fan cools an empty room
misconceptions.correction: Fans cool people, not rooms, so turn them off when you leave.

misconceptions.name: Cooler skin means cooler air

steps.title: A fan moves air; it adds no cold

hook.stem: A ceiling fan runs in a warm hostel room. Where does its breeze come from?

options.text: The room's own air, pushed by the blades.
options.feedback: Right. The blades push the air already in the room, so the breeze is room air.

options.text: Cool air made inside the motor.
options.feedback: The motor only spins the blades. A fan makes no cold air.

options.text: Fresh, cooler air drawn in from outside the room.
options.feedback: A ceiling fan only stirs the air already in the room.

steps.teach: A fan's spinning blades push the room's own air along. They add no cold, because a fan only moves air that is already there. Fans that can reverse even push warm ceiling air down in winter.

example.ask: Tap where the breeze comes from.
parts: The fan in the hostel room spins,
its blades push the room's own air down,
so the breeze is as warm as the room.
example.spot: its blades push the room's own air down,
example.feedback: The breeze is just the room's own air on the move, so it is no colder than the room.

guided.stem: A fan blows on a dry steel spoon in a warm room. Does the spoon get colder than the room?
guided.hint: How warm is the air blowing on it?

options.text: No, it stays at room heat.
options.feedback: Right. The fan blows room air, and a dry spoon has nothing to dry, so it stays at room heat.

options.text: Yes, a little colder than the air.
options.feedback: The breeze is room air. With nothing to dry, the spoon cannot drop below it.

options.text: Yes, it turns icy cold.
options.feedback: Moving warm air cannot chill a dry spoon below room heat.

steps.takeaway: A fan moves the room's own air; it adds no cold.

steps.title: Moving air dries sweat, so you feel cooler

hook.stem: A fan blows on you in a hot classroom, yet the air is just as warm. Why do you feel cooler?

options.text: The breeze helps sweat dry off your skin.
options.feedback: Right. Drying sweat takes heat from your skin.

options.text: The fan pulls heat out through the ceiling.
options.feedback: A ceiling fan has no way to send heat out. Drying sweat cools your skin.

options.text: The spinning blades block the warm sunlight.
options.feedback: Shade is not the reason. Drying sweat cools your skin.

steps.teach: As sweat dries off your skin, it carries heat away. A breeze makes sweat dry faster, so you feel cooler, though the air is no colder. In an empty room, a fan cools no one.

example.ask: Tap what actually cools Rohan.
parts: Rohan sits under the fan after cricket,
the breeze dries the sweat on his arms,
and he feels cooler, though the room is still warm.
example.spot: the breeze dries the sweat on his arms,
example.feedback: Drying sweat is what cools him. The room air itself stays just as warm.

guided.stem: Why does a fan feel cooler on wet skin just after a bath?
guided.hint: Which skin has more to dry?

options.text: More water dries off, taking more heat.
options.feedback: Right. There is more water to dry, so more heat leaves your skin.

options.text: Wet skin makes the fan spin faster.
options.feedback: The fan spins the same. Wet skin just has more water to dry.

options.text: Bath water makes the room air colder.
options.feedback: The air stays warm. Drying water takes heat from your skin.

steps.takeaway: A breeze cools skin mainly by drying sweat, not by chilling air.

steps.title: In humid air, a fan helps less

hook.stem: Same fan, same heat. Why does it feel weaker on a sticky monsoon night than on a dry summer day?

options.text: Wet air slows the drying of sweat.
options.feedback: Right. Humid air is already full of water, so sweat dries slowly and cools you less.

options.text: Fans spin slower when it rains.
options.feedback: The fan spins the same. The damp air is what slows the cooling.

options.text: Monsoon air is too heavy to move.
options.feedback: The fan moves the air fine. Damp air just slows how fast sweat dries.

steps.teach: Humid air already holds a lot of water, so sweat dries off slowly in it. On a sticky monsoon night, the same breeze takes less heat from your skin, so the fan helps less.

example.ask: Tap why the fan helps so little.
parts: On a monsoon night in Chennai, Meera turns the fan up,
but her sweat barely dries in the damp air,
so she still feels hot.
example.spot: but her sweat barely dries in the damp air,
example.feedback: In damp air sweat dries slowly, so the breeze takes little heat from her skin.

guided.stem: Two rooms are both at 34°C. In which one does a fan cool you better?
guided.hint: Where can sweat dry faster?

options.text: The room with drier air.
options.feedback: Right. Sweat dries faster in drier air, so the breeze cools you more.

options.text: The room with damper air.
options.feedback: Damp air slows the drying of sweat, so the fan helps less there.

options.text: Both rooms, just the same.
options.feedback: The heat matches, but drier air lets sweat dry faster, so the fan helps more there.

steps.takeaway: Damp air slows drying sweat, so a fan cools you less.

concepts.title: How UPI moves money
concepts.hook: A UPI ID helps route a payment between bank accounts; the money is not stored in the ID.
concepts.rule: Your UPI ID points to your bank account. You approve a payment on your own phone, usually with your UPI PIN. NPCI's network carries it, and the two banks move the money, at any hour. If you are tricked, call 1930.

claims.text: A UPI ID is a payment address that you set, and it points to your linked bank account.
UPI moves money between bank accounts, and NPCI runs the network that links the banks.
UPI works all day, every day of the year, and the money reaches the payee at once. The banks settle with each other later, a few times a day.
A UPI payment is checked two ways: your registered phone, and an approval, usually your UPI PIN.
Getting money never needs a QR scan or your PIN.
With a UPI ID, you do not need the other person's account number or IFSC code.
UPI handled 16.58 billion payments in October 2024, a month of 31 days.
You can pick any UPI app, whichever bank holds your account.
Some apps let you approve payments up to ₹5,000 with a fingerprint or face instead of the UPI PIN.
From 1 October 2025, UPI no longer lets one person send another a request to pay.

items.stem: Your email address lets people send you mail but not open your inbox. Which is true of your UPI ID too?

options.text: It lets people send you money, not take it.
options.feedback: Like an email address, a UPI ID tells others where to send. Taking money needs your own approval.

options.text: It lets anyone who has it see your bank balance.
options.feedback: The ID only points to your account. It shows no balance to anyone.

options.text: It lets people pay themselves from your account.
options.feedback: Money leaves only when you approve on your own phone. The ID is just an address.

items.stem: Neha typed the right amount, but the money reached a stranger instead of her friend. What did she most likely get wrong?

options.text: The UPI ID she sent it to.
options.feedback: The ID is the address that decides whose bank gets the money, so a wrong ID sends it to someone else.

options.text: Her UPI PIN, which she typed slowly.
options.feedback: A wrong PIN stops the payment. It cannot send money to another person.

options.text: The time of day she sent it.
options.feedback: UPI works at any hour. The address, her friend's UPI ID, decides where money goes.

items.stem: At midnight, Asha pays ₹30 at the college canteen by UPI. The banks settle up with each other only a few times a day. When does the canteen's account get the money?

options.text: At once, while the banks settle later.
options.feedback: The payee is paid straight away. The banks square up between themselves later, in set rounds each day.

options.text: At the next bank settlement round.
options.feedback: Settlement is between the banks. The canteen gets the money straight away.

options.text: When the bank branch opens in the morning.
options.feedback: UPI does not wait for branch hours. The canteen is paid at once, any time.

items.stem: UPI's network carries payments every hour of every day. In one month of 31 days it carried about 16.58 billion payments. About how many million is that per day?

options.text: About 535 million.
options.feedback: 16.58 billion is 16,580 million. Over 31 days that is about 535 million payments a day.

options.text: About 16 million.
options.feedback: That mixes up millions and billions. 16,580 million over 31 days is about 535 million a day.

options.text: About 5 billion.
options.feedback: Too big. 16.58 billion over 31 days is about 535 million a day, about half a billion.

items.stem: Before money leaves by UPI, two things are checked. One is your UPI PIN, or your fingerprint for a small sum. The other is ___.

options.text: your own registered phone.
options.feedback: UPI checks the phone linked to your account as well as your approval, so a stolen PIN alone is not enough.

options.text: the payee's bank balance.
options.feedback: The payee's balance is not checked. Your own phone and your approval are the two checks.

options.text: a call from your bank.
options.feedback: No call is needed. Your registered phone and your approval are the two checks.

items.stem: A stranger sends Rohan a QR code: 'Scan it and enter your UPI PIN to get your ₹2,000 refund.' Predict what happens if he does.

options.text: ₹2,000 leaves his account.
options.feedback: Scanning and entering a PIN approves a payment out. A real refund needs no scan and no PIN. If tricked, call 1930.

options.text: ₹2,000 comes into his account.
options.feedback: Getting money never needs a scan or a PIN. Entering it pays the stranger instead.

options.text: No money moves until his bank calls him.
options.feedback: Entering the PIN approves the payment at once. Strangers can no longer send collect requests, but a QR code can still ask you to pay.

misconceptions.correction: The app starts the request while NPCI's network and the banks do the transfer.

misconceptions.correction: Getting money never needs your PIN or a QR scan.

concepts.title: How a phone camera takes a photo
concepts.hook: A camera lens aims light at a sensor. Millions of tiny light readings are then turned into a photo.
concepts.rule: A phone lens aims light at a sensor chip. Each tiny spot turns light into a signal, colour filters sort red, green and blue, and software builds the photo. In dim light the phone boosts the signal, which adds grain.

claims.text: Each tiny spot in a phone sensor turns light into a signal, and more light gives a bigger signal.
A filter grid with 1 red, 2 green and 1 blue square in each 2x2 patch lets the phone work out colour.
Software uses the filter pattern to work out a full colour for every pixel.
Turning up ISO multiplies the signal but does not make the sensor more sensitive, so a high ISO in dim light gives a bright but grainy photo.
Most phone cameras have a fixed lens opening, so a phone sets brightness with ISO and with how long the shutter stays open.
Doubling the time the shutter stays open and halving the ISO gives the same exposure.

items.stem: Diya says the lens of her phone is what records her selfie. What is not quite right?

options.text: The lens only aims light; the sensor chip records it.
options.feedback: The lens gathers and aims light. The tiny spots on the sensor chip turn it into signals.

options.text: The lens records it, but just in daylight.
options.feedback: The lens never records anything. The sensor chip turns light into signals.

options.text: The screen records it as you look at the preview.
options.feedback: The screen only shows the photo. The sensor chip recorded the light.

items.stem: In a photo, one patch of a wall looks much brighter than the rest. What does that tell you about the sensor spots that saw it?

options.text: More light reached them, so their signals were bigger.
options.feedback: Brightness in the photo comes from signal size, and a bigger signal means more light landed there.

options.text: Those spots were newer and simply worked better.
options.feedback: The spots are alike. A brighter patch means more light reached them.

options.text: Software made that patch brighter to fill in a missing gap.
options.feedback: Software fills in colour, but the brightness comes from how much light landed.

items.stem: A phone sensor has 48 million spots under a red, green and blue filter grid. About how many million of them are green?

options.text: About 24 million.
options.feedback: Two of every four spots are green, so half of 48 million is 24 million.

options.text: About 16 million.
options.feedback: That splits the spots evenly in three. Green gets half, about 24 million.

options.text: About 12 million.
options.feedback: A quarter is the share for red or for blue. Green gets half, 24 million.

items.stem: Why can a photo show a full colour at every pixel when each spot sees only one colour?

options.text: Software works out the missing colours from nearby spots.
options.feedback: Each spot gives a signal through one filter. Software uses the pattern of nearby signals to estimate full colour.

options.text: Each spot quietly records the three colours at the same time.
options.feedback: Each spot sees light through one filter only. Software fills in the rest.

options.text: The lens paints the colour onto each pixel.
options.feedback: The lens only aims light. The colour is worked out by software.

items.stem: At a college star-gazing night, Tanvi sets the phone on a stand, keeps the shutter open for many seconds and uses a low ISO. Predict the photo.

options.text: Bright and fairly clean, with little grain.
options.feedback: The long shot gathers enough light, so the phone needs little boost. The stand stops shake from blurring it.

options.text: Dark and very grainy, like any night photo.
options.feedback: Night photos are grainy when the signal is boosted. Here the long shot gathers light instead.

options.text: Blurred from the long shot.
options.feedback: Blur comes from shake. On a stand, the long shot stays sharp.

items.stem: On a video call from a dim hostel room, Priya's face looks speckled to her friends. What is the webcam doing?

options.text: Boosting a weak signal, which adds grain.
options.feedback: Any camera in dim light has a weak signal. Turning it up brightens her face but adds speckle.

options.text: Sending fewer pixels because the call is slow.
options.feedback: A slow call can blur a picture, but speckle in dim light comes from boosting.

options.text: Showing that the webcam is broken.
options.feedback: Grain in dim light is normal. More light on her face would clean it up.

misconceptions.name: Grain means a broken camera
misconceptions.correction: Grain often comes from boosting a weak signal in dim light.

misconceptions.name: Lens records the image
misconceptions.correction: The lens directs light, while the sensor records the signal.

misconceptions.name: Each pixel sees every colour
misconceptions.correction: Each spot reads light through one colour filter; software fills in the rest.

misconceptions.name: A longer shot is always better
misconceptions.correction: Keeping the shutter open longer gathers light, but any shake while it is open can blur the photo.

steps.title: Each sensor spot turns light into a signal

hook.stem: What does one tiny spot on a phone's camera sensor measure?

options.text: How much light lands on it.
options.feedback: Right. Each spot turns the light that hits it into a signal.

options.text: The colour of the object directly.
options.feedback: A spot only measures light. Colour comes from filters on top.

options.text: How far away the object is.
options.feedback: The spot measures light, not distance.

steps.teach: The lens aims light onto a chip covered in tiny light sensors. Each one makes an electric signal that grows with the light, so brighter parts of the scene give bigger signals.

example.ask: Tap where light becomes a signal.
parts: Light from Diya's face passes through the lens,
hits the tiny sensors on the chip,
and the phone builds a selfie from their signals.
