example.feedback: The sensors on the chip turn light into signals. The lens only aims the light.

guided.stem: One sensor spot gets twice as much light as the spot next to it, in the same time. What about its signal?
guided.hint: How does the signal follow the light?

options.text: About twice as big.
options.feedback: Right. The signal grows in step with the light that hits it.

options.text: About the same, since spots match.
options.feedback: The spots are alike, but more light still gives a bigger signal.

options.text: About half as big.
options.feedback: More light means more signal, not less.

steps.takeaway: Each sensor spot turns light into a signal.

steps.title: Colour comes from a filter grid

hook.stem: Can a single sensor spot tell red from blue on its own?

options.text: No, a colour filter over it does that.
options.feedback: Right. Each spot sees light through one red, green or blue filter.

options.text: Yes, each spot sees the colours at once.
options.feedback: A bare spot only measures brightness. Filters sort the colours.

options.text: Yes, but just in bright daylight.
options.feedback: Daylight does not change this. Filters over the spots sort colour.

steps.teach: Each spot measures only brightness, so colour comes from a grid of tiny filters on top. In every 2x2 patch, two are green, one red and one blue. Software then fills in a full colour for each pixel.

right.title: Then software
lines: Works out full colour for each pixel

example.ask: Tap what gives each spot its colour.
parts: Light reaches the sensor chip,
a red, green or blue filter covers each spot,
and software mixes the readings into colours.
example.spot: a red, green or blue filter covers each spot,
example.feedback: The filter over each spot lets through one colour, so its reading stands for that colour.

guided.stem: A spot under a red filter reads bright. What did it see?
guided.hint: What does a red filter let through?

options.text: Lots of red light.
options.feedback: Right. A bright reading under a red filter means lots of red light.

options.text: Lots of blue light.
options.feedback: A red filter blocks blue, so the bright reading means red light.

options.text: Very little light of any colour.
options.feedback: A bright reading means plenty of light got through, and here it was red.

steps.takeaway: Filters give colour; two of every four spots are green.

steps.title: Dim light means a weak signal and more grain

hook.stem: You take a photo in a dark hostel corridor and it looks grainy. Why?

options.text: The phone boosted a weak signal.
options.feedback: Right. Boosting a weak signal turns up the speckle too, so the photo looks grainy.

options.text: The lens got smudged in the dark room.
options.feedback: Darkness does not dirty a lens. Grain comes from boosting a weak signal.

options.text: Dark photos use fewer pixels.
options.feedback: Grain comes from boosting a weak signal, not from losing pixels.

steps.teach: In dim light each spot gets little light, so its signal is weak. The phone turns the signal up (ISO), but that turns up the random speckle too, so the photo looks grainy.

example.ask: Tap the cause of the grain.
parts: At a night wedding, Kabir snaps the stage,
his phone pushes ISO very high,
so the dark parts look speckled.
example.spot: his phone pushes ISO very high,
example.feedback: A very high ISO boosts the weak signal, and that boost shows up as speckled grain.

guided.stem: Same dark room. Instead of a high ISO, the phone keeps its shutter open longer. What is the risk?
guided.hint: What if you shake while it is still taking the shot?

options.text: Blur if your hand moves.
options.feedback: Right. A longer shot gathers more light with less boost, but any shake while it is open smears the photo.

options.text: More grain than a high ISO.
options.feedback: A longer shot needs less boost, so it usually has less grain. Shake is the risk.

options.text: Colours swap between red and blue.
options.feedback: The filters stay the same. The risk of a long shot is blur from shake.

steps.takeaway: Less light means a weak signal, and boosting it adds grain.

concepts.title: Blue sky and red sunsets
concepts.hook: Air scatters blue light more than red. At sunset, light takes a long path through the air, so mostly red gets through.
concepts.rule: Sunlight is a mix of colours. Air scatters short blue waves far more than long red ones, so the sky looks blue. Near sunset, a longer path through air removes more blue from direct sunlight.

claims.text: Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more easily in Earth's air than red ones.
At sunrise and sunset, sunlight takes a longer path through the air, so mostly the yellow-to-red part reaches us.
Sunlight is a mix of colours, and each colour is a different wavelength, so a prism can spread them apart.
Violet waves are the shortest we see, about 380 nm long. Red waves are the longest, about 700 nm.
The Moon has no air, so its sky looks black even in bright sunshine.
Cloud droplets are much bigger than air molecules and scatter all colours about the same, so clouds look white.
In a lunar eclipse, the Moon looks red or orange because the sunlight reaching it is filtered through a thick slice of Earth's air.
A few drops of milk in water scatter blue light from a torch, much as air molecules do.
Clouds or air pollution can make a sunset even redder, since the particles scatter away more short waves.

items.stem: A classmate says a glass prism adds colours to white light. What is not quite right?

options.text: The colours were already in the light; the prism spreads them out.
options.feedback: Each colour is a different wavelength, and the prism sends each a slightly different way.

options.text: The prism adds colours, but just when sunlight is strong.
options.feedback: A prism adds nothing. It spreads out colours already mixed into white light.

options.text: The prism takes away the white and leaves black.
options.feedback: White light becomes a band of colours, not black, because it was a mix all along.

items.stem: Light we can see runs from violet, past blue and green, to red. A red wave is about 700 nm long, about 1.84 times as long as a violet wave. About how long is a violet wave, in nm?

options.text: About 380 nm.
options.feedback: 700 divided by 1.84 is about 380, which is where violet sits at the short end.

options.text: About 1,290 nm.
options.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing. Violet is the shorter wave, about 380 nm.

options.text: About 700 nm.
options.feedback: That is the red wave. Violet is much shorter, about 380 nm.

items.stem: Why is the daytime sky on the Moon black, not blue?

options.text: There is no air to scatter the sunlight.
options.feedback: The blue sky comes from air scattering sunlight. With no air, nothing scatters it, so the sky stays black.

options.text: Less blue light reaches the Moon from the Sun.
options.feedback: The same sunlight reaches the Moon. It has no air to scatter the blue.

options.text: Grey Moon dust soaks up the blue light.
options.feedback: Dust is not the cause. With no air, nothing scatters the light toward the eye.

items.stem: In the hostel kitchen, Raj shines a phone torch through a glass of water with a few drops of milk in it. From the side, the water looks bluish. Why?

options.text: Tiny milk bits scatter the blue light sideways.
options.feedback: The milk bits act like air molecules, scattering blue from the white torch light toward his eye.

options.text: The milk turns slightly blue once it mixes with water.
options.feedback: Milk is white. The bits scatter the blue part of the torch light.

options.text: The torch gives out mostly blue light.
options.feedback: The torch light is white. The milk scatters its blue part sideways.

items.stem: A cricket match runs from noon until the Sun sets. Predict how the low Sun looks near the end.

options.text: More orange and red.
options.feedback: Near sunset, light crosses more air, so the blue scatters away and reds are left.

options.text: More blue and violet.
options.feedback: The long path removes blue, so the low Sun looks redder, not bluer.

options.text: Just the same as at noon.
options.feedback: The path through air gets longer, which shifts the Sun toward red.

items.stem: In a total lunar eclipse, Earth blocks the direct sunlight, and the only light reaching the Moon skims through the air at Earth's edge. Why does the Moon then look red?

options.text: Earth's air scatters out the blue, so red light reaches it.
options.feedback: Air scatters blue, and the long path through the edge of Earth's air leaves mostly red light for the Moon.

options.text: The Moon heats up and glows red in the dark.
options.feedback: The Moon does not glow. It is lit by sunlight filtered through Earth's air.

options.text: The light passes through Earth's oceans and turns red.
options.feedback: Light cannot pass through Earth. It skims through the air at Earth's edge.

misconceptions.name: Sky is blue paint
misconceptions.correction: The colour comes from scattered sunlight, not dye in the air.

misconceptions.name: Sun turns red
misconceptions.correction: The same Sun is seen through a longer path of air near the horizon.

misconceptions.name: A prism adds the colours
misconceptions.correction: White sunlight is already a mix; a prism only spreads the colours apart.

steps.title: Sunlight is a mix of colours

hook.stem: Sunlight looks white. What is it really made of?

options.text: A mix of all the rainbow colours.
options.feedback: Right. White sunlight is a blend of colours, from violet to red.

options.text: Pure yellow light from the hot Sun.
options.feedback: Sunlight holds every rainbow colour, not just yellow.

options.text: One white colour of its own.
options.feedback: White is not one colour. Sunlight is a mix of all the colours.

steps.teach: White sunlight is a blend of colours, from violet to red. Each colour is a wave with its own length, so a prism can spread them apart: red waves are long, violet and blue are short.

example.ask: Tap the colours hidden in sunlight.
parts: Sunlight passes through a glass prism,
and spreads into a band of rainbow colours,
so white light was a mix all along.
example.spot: and spreads into a band of rainbow colours,
example.feedback: The prism spreads sunlight into its colours, showing that white light is a mix.

guided.stem: Which colour of light has the longer wavelength?
guided.hint: Which end of the rainbow has the long waves?

options.text: Red.
options.feedback: Right. Red has a long wavelength, and blue a much shorter one.

options.text: Blue.
options.feedback: Blue waves are short. Red has the longer wavelength.

options.text: They are the same.
options.feedback: Each colour has its own length. Red is longer than blue.

steps.takeaway: White light is a mix; blue waves are short, red waves long.

steps.title: Air scatters blue far more than red

hook.stem: Why is a clear daytime sky blue?

options.text: Air scatters blue sunlight across the sky.
options.feedback: Right. Air molecules scatter short blue waves in all directions.

options.text: The sky reflects the colour of the blue sea.
options.feedback: The sky is blue far from any sea. Air scatters blue sunlight.

options.text: Air is tinted blue, like dye.
options.feedback: Air has no blue dye. It scatters blue sunlight to us.

steps.teach: Gas molecules in the air bounce short blue waves in all directions, so blue reaches you from all over the sky. Red waves mostly pass straight through. Big cloud droplets scatter every colour about the same, so clouds look white.

example.ask: Tap why the whole sky glows blue.
parts: Sunlight streams over a school at noon,
air molecules scatter its blue waves every way,
so blue reaches students from all over the sky.
example.spot: air molecules scatter its blue waves every way,
example.feedback: Air scatters the blue waves in every direction, so blue comes at you from the whole sky.

guided.stem: Why do clouds look white, not blue?
guided.hint: How big are the bits in a cloud?

options.text: Their big droplets scatter every colour.
options.feedback: Right. Droplets far bigger than air molecules scatter all colours about the same, which looks white.

options.text: Clouds are made of white dust.
options.feedback: Clouds are water droplets. They look white because they scatter all colours.

options.text: Clouds hold back the blue and let the white through.
options.feedback: Big droplets scatter every colour about the same, so the mix looks white.

steps.takeaway: Air scatters short blue waves all over the sky.

steps.title: A long path at sunset leaves the reds

hook.stem: Near sunset, the Sun looks orange. What changed?

options.text: Its light crosses much more air.
options.feedback: Right. The longer path through air scatters away the blue.

options.text: The Sun cools down a little each evening.
options.feedback: The Sun is the same. Its light just crosses more air to reach you.

options.text: The Sun moved farther away.
options.feedback: The Sun is the same distance away. Its light just crosses more air.

steps.teach: When the Sun is low, its light crosses far more air to reach you. Along the way, most of the blue is scattered out, so mostly reds and oranges are left.

example.ask: Tap why the Sun looks red.
parts: From a train window, Om watches the evening Sun,
its light crosses a long stretch of air,
and mostly reds and oranges get through.
example.spot: its light crosses a long stretch of air,
example.feedback: The long path through air scatters out the blue, so reds and oranges are left.

guided.stem: Smoke or dust fills the air at sunset. What can happen to the colours?
guided.hint: More bits in the air scatter away more short waves.

options.text: The sunset can look even redder.
options.feedback: Right. Smoke and dust can scatter away even more of the shorter waves.

options.text: The sunset turns blue.
options.feedback: Extra particles strip out more blue, so the sunset gets redder.

options.text: The colours stay just as they were.
options.feedback: Particles scatter more short waves, which can deepen the reds.

steps.takeaway: A longer path through air scatters out blue, leaving red.

concepts.title: Pressure cooker
concepts.hook: A sealed cooker raises pressure, so water can boil at a higher temperature.
concepts.rule: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point. A sealed cooker reaches about 121°C, so food cooks faster. Its vent weight lets out steam to hold the pressure steady. Keep the vent clear and open the lid only once the pressure has dropped.

claims.text: Water boils at a higher temperature when the pressure on it is higher, and at a lower one when the pressure is lower.
A pressure cooker cooks faster because its higher pressure raises the boiling point of the water inside.
A typical cooker vents at about double the outside pressure, so its water boils near 121°C.
Air pressure is lower up high, so water boils cooler: about 95°C at 5,000 feet (about 1,500 m) and 89°C at 10,000 feet (about 3,000 m).
While water is boiling, its temperature stays the same; more heat only boils it off faster.
Cookers made to the Indian standard hold the pressure with a free dead weight on the vent, plus a separate safety device.
The 2006 Indian standard's instructions say to fill a cooker no more than two thirds full, or half full for foods that swell, and warn that frothy food can block the vent.
Burns from steam are usually worse than burns from boiling water.

items.stem: On a college trek high in the hills, the group's dal takes far longer to soften in an open pot than at home. What best explains it?

options.text: Water boils below 100°C up there, so it cooks cooler.
options.feedback: Lower air pressure up high lowers the boiling point, and cooler water softens dal more slowly.

options.text: Thin mountain air lets the pot's heat escape much faster.
options.feedback: Heat loss is not the main issue. The water itself boils cooler up high.

options.text: Hill water is harder, so the dal soaks it up slowly.
options.feedback: The water is not the problem. It boils at a lower temperature up high.

items.stem: Water boils at 100°C on the plains and near 89°C about 3,000 m up, where air pressure is lower. Tara turns up the flame in a town about 1,500 m up. About what temperature does her water boil at?

options.text: About 95°C.
options.feedback: At about 1,500 m water boils near 95°C, halfway between. A bigger flame cannot push it higher.

options.text: 100°C, with a big enough flame.
options.feedback: Flame cannot raise a boil. With lower air pressure there, it boils near 95°C.

options.text: About 89°C.
options.feedback: That is the boil about 3,000 m up. Halfway up, it is about 95°C.

items.stem: Sana says a cooker is faster because pressure squeezes flavour and heat into the food. What is not quite right?

options.text: Pressure raises the boiling point; hotter water cooks faster.
options.feedback: The extra pressure lets water boil near 121°C, and that heat is what cooks food faster.

options.text: Pressure squeezes heat in, and also raises the boil.
options.feedback: Pressure works by raising the boiling point, not by squeezing heat in.

options.text: Cookers are faster just for beans like rajma.
options.feedback: Any food in the hotter water cooks faster, not only beans.

items.stem: Why do climbers cooking high in the Himalayas often use pressure cookers?

options.text: Sealing the pot lifts the boil back up, so food can cook.
options.feedback: Up high, an open pot boils too cool to cook well. A cooker raises the pressure and so the boiling point.

options.text: Ordinary pots crack in the cold, thin mountain air up there.
options.feedback: Cracking is not the reason. Up high, open water boils too cool to cook well.

options.text: Pressure cookers weigh less, so they are easy to carry.
options.feedback: Weight is not the point. The sealed pot raises the boiling point that the thin air lowered.

items.stem: Put the steps of a cooker's whistle in order.

options.text: Steam builds and the pressure rises.
options.feedback: First, heating the sealed cooker makes steam, and the pressure climbs.

options.text: The pressure lifts the vent weight.
options.feedback: Next, at its set pressure, the steam pushes the weight up.

options.text: Steam escapes with a whistle.
options.feedback: Then steam rushes out past the lifted weight, which makes the whistle.

options.text: The pressure stops climbing and holds steady.
options.feedback: Last, the escaping steam stops the pressure rising any further.

items.stem: In the hostel kitchen, Kunal fills a cooker almost to the top with rice and water. What is the risk?

options.text: Swelling rice and froth can block the vent, so steam cannot escape.
options.feedback: Steam keeps building pressure while a blocked vent cannot let it out. Fill rice and other swelling foods at most half full.

options.text: The rice cooks so fast it sticks to the bottom of the pot.
options.feedback: Sticking is a small worry. The real risk is a blocked vent while the pressure builds.

options.text: The extra water keeps the cooker from ever reaching full pressure.
options.feedback: More water still turns to steam and builds pressure. Froth from swelling rice can block the vent.

misconceptions.name: Pressure pushes flavour in
misconceptions.correction: The extra push lets the water boil at a higher heat.

misconceptions.name: More flame raises an open boil
misconceptions.correction: Boiling water stays at the same heat, however big the flame.

misconceptions.name: The whistle only says food is done
misconceptions.correction: The vent weight lets out steam to hold the pressure steady.

misconceptions.name: Fill it up to save time
misconceptions.correction: Food that swells or froths can block the vent, so swelling foods go in at most half full.

steps.title: The boiling point depends on pressure

hook.stem: Trekkers high on a mountain boil water for tea. Guess how hot the boiling water gets.

options.text: Below 100°C.
options.feedback: Right. Lower air pressure up high makes water boil below 100°C.

options.text: At 100°C, as at home.
options.feedback: 100°C is the boil near sea level. Up high, water boils cooler.

options.text: Above 100°C.
options.feedback: That needs more pressure, as in a cooker. Up high it is less.

steps.teach: Air presses down on water, and the harder it presses, the hotter water must get to boil. So on hills water boils below 100°C. Once boiling, more flame only boils it off faster; it gets no hotter.

example.ask: Tap why the dal cooks slowly.
parts: In a hill town, Tenzin boils dal in an open pot,
the thin air lets the water boil below 100°C,
so the dal takes longer to soften.
example.spot: the thin air lets the water boil below 100°C,
example.feedback: Lower air pressure on hills lowers the boiling point, so the cooler water cooks slowly.

guided.stem: An open pot of water is boiling hard. You turn the flame up. What happens to the water's temperature?
guided.hint: Watch what extra heat does once boiling starts.

options.text: It stays about the same.
options.feedback: Right. While it boils, its temperature stays put; it just boils off faster.

options.text: It rises past 120°C.
options.feedback: An open pot cannot boil that hot. The temperature stays the same.

options.text: It drops a little.
options.feedback: More flame does not cool it. The temperature stays the same.

steps.takeaway: Less pressure, cooler boil; more pressure, hotter boil.

steps.title: A sealed cooker boils hotter

hook.stem: A pressure cooker traps steam. About how hot can its boiling water get?

options.text: About 121°C.
options.feedback: Right. At working pressure, water boils near 121°C.

options.text: About 100°C.
options.feedback: That is an open pot. Trapped steam lifts the boil to about 121°C.

options.text: About 200°C.
options.feedback: Too high. A home cooker boils water near 121°C.

steps.teach: A sealed cooker traps steam, so the pressure inside builds up. At about double the outside pressure, water boils near 121°C instead of 100°C. Hotter water cooks food faster.

example.ask: Tap why the rajma cooks faster.
parts: Kabir seals the rajma in the pressure cooker,
the trapped steam lets the water reach about 121°C,
so the beans soften in far less time.
example.spot: the trapped steam lets the water reach about 121°C,
example.feedback: Trapped steam raises the pressure, so the water gets hotter than 100°C and cooks faster.

guided.stem: Which is hotter: an open pot boiling on a big flame, or a cooker boiling on a low flame?
guided.hint: Does flame or pressure set the boil?

options.text: The cooker.
options.feedback: Right. Its higher pressure lets its water boil near 121°C.

options.text: The open pot.
options.feedback: A big flame cannot push an open boil past 100°C. The cooker is hotter.

options.text: Both the same.
options.feedback: The cooker's pressure makes its water hotter than the open pot.

steps.takeaway: Trapped steam raises pressure, so water boils near 121°C.

steps.title: The vent weight keeps the pressure steady

hook.stem: What does the weight on top of a cooker's vent do?

options.text: Lets out steam to keep the pressure steady.
options.feedback: Right. It lifts at its set pressure and lets steam out.

options.text: Seals the steam inside the cooker until you lift it.
options.feedback: It does the opposite. It lifts and lets steam out at the set pressure.

options.text: Shows when the food is done.
options.feedback: The whistle is steam escaping. Its job is to hold the pressure steady.

steps.teach: The vent weight lifts at high pressure and lets steam out, which is the whistle, so pressure stays steady. Keep the vent clear: fill rice or dried beans at most half full, since froth can block it.

example.ask: Tap what keeps the pressure steady.
parts: The cooker heats up on the stove,
the vent weight lifts and lets out a whistle of steam,
so the pressure inside holds steady.
example.spot: the vent weight lifts and lets out a whistle of steam,
example.feedback: When the weight lifts, extra steam escapes, so the pressure cannot keep climbing.

guided.stem: Cooking is done, but the cooker is still under pressure. What is the safe step?
guided.hint: What must happen before the lid is safe?

options.text: Wait until the pressure has fully dropped.
options.feedback: Right. Open the lid only once the cooker has cooled and the pressure is gone.

options.text: Force the lid open quickly.
options.feedback: Never force it. Wait until the pressure has fully dropped.

options.text: Tap and shake the cooker hard to free the lid.
options.feedback: Shaking a hot cooker is risky. Wait for the pressure to drop.

steps.takeaway: Weight holds pressure steady; keep the vent clear, never force the lid.
